title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Journal (5 min)
Choose one option and write silently. We’ll hear from a couple of people afterward.


Option A
Think of the most linguistically diverse place you’ve spent real time in — a family gathering, a workplace, a neighborhood, a market. How many languages were in the air? What did it feel like to be surrounded by that much variety?

Option B
Now think of the opposite — a place where just about everyone around you spoke the same way. Did that sameness stand out to you at the time, or only looking back on it now?


~5 min: 4 min silent writing, then 1-2 volunteers share. Personal/experiential prompts, not fact-based. Bridge into the next slide: “some of you described Option A places, some Option B — that split tracks a real pattern.”

section: WA1 Proposals: Takeaways for Your Draft

WA1 Proposals: Takeaways for Your Draft

Name a specific concept — the strongest proposals cited an actual course term or reading, not just “language stuff we talked about.”
Pick ONE throughline — several proposals bundled two or three angles at once. For 750 words, narrowing to one story now makes the Draft easier.
Word count is a guide, not a wall — plenty of you went past ~200 words on the proposal, which is fine. It just isn’t required.
Anchor in one concrete scene — the strongest proposals are built around a specific moment, not a general description.


~4 min. Quick, whole-class debrief on WA1 proposals before diving into new content — not individual feedback, just the patterns worth naming out loud. Keep this brisk and encouraging.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
section: How Many Languages? PNG vs. Samoa
text:
How Many Languages? PNG vs. Samoa


843
languages in Papua New Guinea — the most linguistically diverse country on Earth (2025/26 count), ahead of Indonesia’s ~709.

1
indigenous language in Samoa. (Compare: Vanuatu ~100, Solomon Islands ~63, all of Micronesia ~16, all of Fiji/Polynesia ~22 combined.)


Pair-share (2 min): Walking through a market in Port Moresby, Honiara, or Port Vila, you might hear twenty languages before you finish shopping. In Apia, maybe two. Why would that be so different? Don’t look it up — just guess with a partner.


~7 min. Bridge from the journal: “some of you just described Option A places, some described Option B — turns out that split tracks a real, measurable pattern.” Then Lynch’s market scenario, pair-share on WHY before moving on.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Four Kinds of Pacific Languages







Category
Description




① Indigenous
Native to the country or territory — what most of this course has focused on so far.


② Metropolitan
The colonial or national language of government, education, and formal life — usually English, sometimes French, Spanish, or Indonesian.


③ Pidgin / Creole
Contact languages like Bislama, Tok Pisin, Pijin — covered in depth Thursday.


④ Immigrant
Languages brought by more recent arrivals. Lynch sets this aside in the chapter — keep it in mind for Fiji.




~4 min framing. New content from Ch.7 §2. Flag pidgin-creole is a quick callback only. End by flagging Fiji Hindi as a preview — technically “immigrant” by this framework, yet functions almost like a metropolitan language.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Vanuatu vs. Samoa


Team Vanuatu

~100 indigenous languages, ~250,000 people
Jointly ruled by England & France until 1980 — both English and French are official
Bislama spoken by ~95% of the population
Typical ni-Vanuatu speaks 3+ languages: local language at home, Bislama in town, English or French at school/work
Port Vila: ~85% of the country’s languages have some speakers there


Team Samoa

1 indigenous language: Samoan
Former German colony (to WWI), independent from New Zealand since 1962
Just two languages in daily use: Samoan and English
Samoan is the medium of instruction in primary school
English = formal/modern settings; Samoan = basically everywhere else



~3 min setup. Split the room in half: Team Vanuatu and Team Samoa. Each group gets their fact sheet and 5 minutes to script a “day in the life.”

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Vanuatu vs. Samoa: Activity Instructions

Script it — narrate one full day, naming which language gets used at each moment.
Assign roles — 1-2 narrators, and actors if you want to act out an exchange.
Perform — 2-3 minutes per group.
Compare — what would be hardest about the other country’s day? Easiest?


~10 min: 5 min group prep, then 2-3 min per group to perform. Debrief: what does it feel like to switch that often vs. barely at all?

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Fiji: The In-Between Case

Fijian — actually a dialect chain; eastern/western and northern/southern speakers don’t always understand each other. A standardized eastern variety is used officially.
Rotuman — spoken on Rotuma, part of Fiji but its own language, related to Fijian but distinct.
Fiji Hindi — brought by Indian indentured laborers in the late 1800s.


~4 min. New territory. Introduce Fiji as the messy in-between case. Three-way split sets up the Fiji Hindi deep-dive next.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Fiji Hindi


~60,000
Indian indentured laborers (girmitiyas) brought to Fiji 1879–1916 on 5-year contracts to work sugarcane

~350,000
descendants in Fiji today — about 30% of the country’s population

“Fiji Baat”
the resulting language, mainly from Awadhi and Bhojpuri — now an official language of Fiji (as “Hindi”)


Language attitudes, again: Fiji Hindi is often looked down on by speakers of Standard Hindi/Urdu as “broken” or “inferior” — even though linguists are clear it’s a full, rule-governed language, not a degraded one. Same pattern we’ve seen with Pidgin/Creole attitudes.


~8 min. This is the expanded section — spend real time here.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Fiji Hindi: Girmit History


May 14, 1879
the ship Leonidas arrives at Levuka from Calcutta with the first 463 indentured laborers

37 years
1879–1916: the full span of Indian indentured emigration to Fiji, ~60,500+ people total

5-year contracts
“Girmit” is a mispronunciation of “agreement” — now the name for the whole era


Today: May 14 is observed as Girmit Day by Indo-Fijian communities in Fiji and the diaspora.


~5 min. Concrete historical anchor — a specific ship, date, and number of people rather than just aggregate stats.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Discussion: Fiji

Fiji has real internal diversity — the Fijian dialect chain plus Rotuman — that looks more like the Melanesian pattern.
But a standardized Fijian and English both function as unifying, public-life languages — more like the Polynesia/Micronesia pattern.
And then there’s Fiji Hindi — a whole additional layer neither pattern predicts, because it’s about 19th-century indentured labor migration, not indigenous settlement history.


Discuss: What does Fiji teach us about the limits of a two-category explanation?


~4 min discussion. Cold-call or pair-share.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
The Telephone Tree

Four communities, one ancestor — split into 4 groups. Everyone starts with: “The octopus stole my sandwich at the market.”
Pass it down — telephone-style within each group, several rounds, no writing anything down.
A later split — split each of the 4 groups in half again, run one more short round within each half.
Compare all eight — write all 8 final versions on the board. Which resemble each other? Which drifted furthest?


~12-15 min. This models Lynch’s Figure 1 (branching diversification) experientially, no phonetics required.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Telephone Tree: Debrief

Notice: the two halves that split from the same group later usually still sound more alike than the more distantly split groups. That’s exactly the branching pattern behind real language families.



~50,000 yrs — settlement in parts of Melanesia (New Guinea region)

~3,000 yrs — oldest settlements in Polynesia/Micronesia

~1,000 yrs — since Hawaiʻi and New Zealand were first settled


~4 min debrief + bridge. More “rounds” = more drift = more languages.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Three Explanatory Factors


① Time
More generations = more drift (just modeled with Telephone Tree).

② Separation
Geographic AND social isolation. Surprise: the sea is often NOT a barrier — coastal communities across a strait can be more similar than communities on the same island.

③ Social Structure
Polynesian societies: large, hierarchical — holds one language together. Melanesian societies: small, egalitarian — harder to keep one language unified.


~5 min mini-lecture.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Activity: Apply the Three Factors

In small groups: you’ll be assigned one of the three factors. In 4 minutes, come up with your own real-world example — Pacific or not — of that factor driving language or dialect divergence. Lynch’s own examples: Canadian vs. European French, or regional US English.


What’s your example?
What kept the groups apart (or together) long enough for the difference to take hold?
Could you imagine it eventually producing two fully separate languages?


~8 min. Groups of 3-4, each assigned one factor, share out ~3 min.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Vanuatu: A 2025 Research Update


72%
of Vanuatu’s indigenous languages are spoken by fewer than 1,000 people

1
Vanuatu language has more than 10,000 speakers — out of nearly 100


A September 2025 study found evidence that Bislama itself may now be squeezing out the local languages it coexists with. Does this undercut Lynch’s picture, or fit right alongside it?


~7 min. Complicate Lynch’s rosy multilingualism picture with current research.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Activity: Research a Pacific Country
In your group: research your assigned country/territory on Wikipedia or another reliable source. You have 8 minutes.

New Caledonia
Tonga
Federated States of Micronesia
Indonesian Papua
Solomon Islands
French Polynesia

Answer as a group:

How many indigenous languages does it have? What’s your source?
What’s the metropolitan (colonial/official) language?
Is there a pidgin, creole, or lingua franca used across language groups?
Which of today’s three factors best explains its level of diversity?
Anything that doesn’t fit the patterns we discussed today?


~8 min research time. Groups have laptops. Circulate while they work.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Compare and Contrast

Report — each group gives a 1-2 minute rundown.
Track it — jot each one on the board: indigenous count, metropolitan language, pidgin/creole (y/n), best-fit factor.
Look at the board — once all six are up, look across the whole set together.


Discuss: Which factor came up most often as the best explanation across the six? Did any country not fit neatly into the patterns from today?


~10-12 min: 1-2 min report per group.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Exit Ticket

Which of the three factors — time, separation, or social structure — best explains a pattern of multilingualism (or its absence) in your own family or community?

Take 3 minutes, write silently. Hang onto this — it may help with your autoethnography.
Reading for next class: Ch. 8, Bradshaw — see Lamākū for the schedule.

~4 min. Exit ticket, silent writing.

Final grades will be rounded (e.g., 87.5 → 88 = B+; 92.4 → 92 = A–). Grades will not be curved.


2.2 Participation (10%)
Your participation grade is made up of three components:

Attendance & Journal – I will take attendance at the start of each class, usually with a brief journal prompt. Please bring a physical notebook to every class. Journals must be handwritten. If you have extenuating circumstances requiring you to miss class, contact me as soon as possible.
Lamākū Discussion Posts – You are responsible for 9 discussion posts over the semester, based on a prompt, and released roughly weekly. Each post must be at least 100 words. These posts contribute to your Writing Intensive (WI) requirement.
Syllabus Quiz – A short quiz on the syllabus will be available in Week 1 on Lamākū. It familiarizes you with the course structure and the quiz format.



2.3 Quizzes (10%)
There will be 4 online quizzes administered through Lamākū. Each quiz will be 10 questions (multiple choice, true/false, fill-in-the-blank, and 1–2 short answer questions) with a 1-hour limit and one attempt. Quizzes will be released on Fridays and close the following Monday at 11:55pm. They cover all course reader and lecture material up to that point. Because quizzes close automatically, late submissions receive a score of 0.


2.4 Midterm Exam (20%)
The midterm exam will be held in-class on Tuesday, October 27. It will cover all course reader and lecture material through Week 8. The exam will be 25–30 questions and open-notes (no textbook or internet). A review sheet will be distributed two weeks beforehand.


2.5 Writing Assignment 1 – Language Autoethnography (20%)
The first writing assignment asks you to reflect on your own experiences with language in Hawaiʻi or the Pacific region. This may include reflecting on your family’s language history, your experience of language shift or maintenance, your relationship to a heritage language, or your observations of multilingualism in your community. The autoethnography should connect your personal narrative to course concepts and readings.
WA1 is scaffolded across three stages, each contributing to the assignment grade:

Proposal (10%): ~200 words describing your focus and how it relates to course content. Due Friday, Sep 25.
Draft (30%): Complete first draft of at least 750 words. Due Friday, Oct 9.
Final (60%): Revised final version incorporating instructor feedback. At least 750 words, excluding references. Due Friday, Oct 23.

Detailed instructions will be posted on Lamākū in Week 2.


2.6 Final Paper (25%)
The Final Paper is a focused research paper of at least 2,500 words (excluding references) on one language, country, or island in the Pacific region, on any topic related to one or more course readings and pre-approved by the instructor. The paper must cite at least 7 academic sources using a consistent citation style. The Final Paper replaces a final exam and is due during Finals Week via Lamākū.
Like WA1, the final paper is scaffolded:

Topic Idea (5%): ~100-150 words identifying a topic or a few topics that you would be interested in pursuing. Due Friday, October 30.
Preliminary Sources and Initial Research Question (15%): 3 academic sources that you think might be appropriate to this topic, and why each one fits, along with your initial research question(s), including a short explanation of what you anticipate you will learn. Due Friday, Nov 6.
Draft (25%): Complete first draft of at least 1,750 words. Due Friday, November 20.
Final Paper (45%): Complete revised final version of at least 2,500 words. Due the date and time of our final exam period (Tuesday, Dec 15 9:45 – 11:45 am).
Final Reflection (10%): Submitted at the same time as the final paper, ~300 words reflecting on the process of researching and writing your final paper.

Detailed instructions will be posted on Lamākū in Week 6.


2.7 Final Presentation (15%)
Final Presentations will take place during Weeks 15–16, after your first draft but before your final paper is due. Each student will have a 10-minute slot: 7–8 minutes of presentation plus 2–3 minutes for questions. Sign-up will be via Google Sheets in Week 14. Presentations will be graded on:

Clear research topic/question
Content accuracy and relevance
Use of at least 3 academic sources
Quality and clarity of slides
Presentation flow and organization



2.8 Extra Credit
There is one extra credit opportunity, worth 4% added to your final grade:

Optional 1-on-1 Meeting (Week 14): Meet with me for 7 minutes via Zoom or in-person at my office hours to discuss your Final Paper/Presentation plans. You must have submitted your Initial Research Question on time and be prepared to discuss your topic and presentation ideas.

3. Course Policies

3.1 Lateness Policy
Late writing assignments (WA1, Final Paper Components, Final Paper) will be penalized 5% for each day submitted after the deadline. It is always better to submit late for partial credit than not to submit at all. Quizzes cannot be taken late — they close automatically on Lamākū.


3.2 Academic Honesty
Academic honesty is expected in this course. Academic dishonesty includes plagiarism and cheating. Students who violate the University rules on scholastic dishonesty will be subject to disciplinary penalties, including possible failure in the course and/or dismissal from the University. Policies will be strictly enforced.


3.3 Generative AI Policy
Generative AI tools (including ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and similar) may be used to support your thinking and polish your writing, but not to generate first drafts, summarize readings, or otherwise substitute for your own intellectual work. You are expected to be the primary author of all submitted work. If you use an AI tool in any assignment, you must include a brief statement at the top describing how you used it (e.g., “I used ChatGPT to check for grammatical errors after completing my draft.”) Undisclosed use of AI to produce substantive written content will be treated as academic dishonesty. When in doubt, ask me.
Keep in mind: learning to write is learning to think. Overreliance on AI undermines the development of your own analytical skills — which is the whole point of a writing-intensive course.


3.4 Accessibility and Accommodations (Kōkua)
If you are a student with a disability and have disability-related needs or concerns, please contact the Kōkua program: (808) 956-7511, kokua@hawaii.edu, or in person at the Queen Liliʻuokalani Center for Student Services, Room 013.


3.5 Counseling and Wellness
If you are experiencing personal difficulties or excessive stress and do not feel comfortable speaking with me directly, the UHM Counseling Center is available to you: http://manoa.hawaii.edu/counseling/.


3.6 Title IX
As a UH employee, I am required to promptly report incidents of sex discrimination or sex-based harassment to the Title IX Coordinator. If you have experienced sex discrimination or harassment and wish to speak with someone confidentially, contact the Confidential Mānoa Advocate at manoaadv@hawaii.edu or (808) 956-9499. For more information: https://manoa.hawaii.edu/titleix/resources/.
